title: CUSUM-epsilon: False-Alarm-Calibrated Rollback Thresholds for Runtime Training Stability Controllers

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to test whether sequential change-point tests can improve rollback controllers by reducing false alarms while maintaining detection power. Paper [6] discusses controlling false alarms in sequential change-point detection using CUSUM, aiming to maintain detection reliability, which aligns with the same objective of balancing false alarms and detection power. Paper [10] also addresses sequential change detection with a focus on minimizing detection delay while controlling false alarms, which is substantively equivalent to the purpose here. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces CUSUM-epsilon, a rollback controller using a one-sided CUSUM statistic (allowance k=0.5) on standardized innovations, calibrated to match a nominal rollback rate. Paper [2] develops a one-sided CUSUM chart for detecting changes in the coefficient of variation, which is equivalent in mechanism as it uses a one-sided CUSUM statistic for sequential detection. Paper [6] also uses CUSUM for sequential change-point detection, focusing on controlling false alarms, which matches the mechanism at the primitive level. Paper [8] investigates the CUSUM statistic for change-point detection under negatively associated sequences, which is another substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation calibrates both controllers to a nominal rollback rate (p0=0.2%) and validates their performance on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 with synthetic gradient perturbations over 20 seeds. Paper [6] uses calibration to control false alarm rates in CUSUM-based change-point detection, which matches the evaluation design of calibrating to a nominal rate. Paper [2] evaluates run-length profiles of one-sided CUSUM charts, which is substantively equivalent as it involves calibration and performance validation of CUSUM-based methods. Paper [8] provides finite sample properties of the CUSUM statistic, which aligns with the evaluation design of validating CUSUM-based methods.

### Domain
The contribution operates in runtime training stability control for neural network training. Paper [14] discusses training instability in deep learning systems, characterizing stability as an intrinsic property of learning systems, which falls within the same general application area of training stability control. Paper [22] and Paper [23] also address training instabilities in gradient descent, focusing on stability and optimization dynamics, which are substantively equivalent in domain.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to explain why sequential evidence accumulation fails in this application. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship — that sequential evidence accumulation fails due to detection delay allowing corrupted updates to compound before rollback when perturbations spike >5 sigma above baseline. While many papers discuss sequential change-point detection and CUSUM methods, none directly address this specific failure mode or its explanation. For example, [1], [4], [7], and [9] focus on improving detection methods or controlling false alarms but do not analyze failure modes of sequential evidence accumulation in the context of large perturbations.

### Mechanism
The mechanism identifies detection delay as the dominant harm caused by CUSUM's multi-step evidence accumulation, allowing corrupted updates to compound before rollback when perturbations exceed 5 sigma. Papers such as [4], [7], and [9] discuss CUSUM-based methodologies and detection delay minimization but do not substantively address the specific mechanism of harm due to compounding corrupted updates during large perturbations. For example, [4] minimizes detection delay in a minimax sense but does not analyze the compounding effect of corrupted updates. Similarly, [7] introduces a window-limited CUSUM but focuses on parameter estimation rather than the harm caused by detection delay in extreme perturbations. Thus, no prior paper contains a substantively equivalent mechanism.

The evaluation analyzes the scope of findings for large, immediately-detectable perturbations (>5 sigma) and leaves subtle gradual drift for future work. Papers such as [4], [7], and [9] use similar evaluation designs, including minimax detection delay analysis, false alarm control, and threshold tuning for sequential change detection. For example, [4] characterizes false alarm probabilities and detection delay, and [7] optimizes window size for detection delay. These evaluation designs are substantively equivalent to the scope analysis in the contribution, even though the specific perturbation scale (>5 sigma) differs. The evaluation design is therefore covered.

### Domain
The domain is change-point detection applied to training anomaly detection. Several prior papers, including [1], [4], [7], and [9], work in the general application area of change-point detection, even though they target different specific sub-problems or datasets.
